title: Text Representation: From Vectors to Context
subtitle: Represent text as numbers, from one-hot vectors, bags of words and TF-IDF to word2vec, fastText and the contextual embeddings of transformers, and learn to visualise and question what they encode.
outcomes: Compare one-hot, bag-of-words, TF-IDF and hashed representations, and reproduce scikit-learn's TF-IDF by hand
Implement skip-gram with negative sampling, and train and evaluate word2vec and fastText embeddings with gensim
Handle out-of-vocabulary words with character n-gram embeddings, and build document-level representations
Explain how static and contextual embeddings differ, and use a transformer's contextual vectors to separate word senses
Visualise embedding spaces with PCA and t-SNE, and interpret similarities, analogies and bias with care
prerequisites: NLP Foundations with Python and Corpora, or the same skills: Python, NLTK corpora, tokenisation and subword ideas; Statistical NLP: Models, Parsing and Information Retrieval helps but isn't required. You need Python 3.10 or later with scikit-learn, PyTorch (CPU is fine), gensim, transformers 4.46 or later and Matplotlib. The labs download the Brown corpus, GloVe vectors (66 MB) and DistilBERT (about 270 MB), with the commands given.
description:
Every NLP system has to turn text into numbers, and the choice of representation decides much of what it can learn. This course follows that choice from the simplest vectors to the contextual ones inside today's language models. You'll start with one-hot vectors and see why they can't express similarity, build bags of words and n-gram features, store them sparsely and reproduce scikit-learn's TF-IDF by hand. Then you'll learn dense embeddings by prediction: you'll write skip-gram with negative sampling in PyTorch, train word2vec with gensim and compare it with pre-trained GloVe vectors.

Next you'll handle the words a model has never seen with fastText's character n-grams, and move from words to documents with averaged vectors and Doc2Vec. You'll open up a transformer encoder, learning the idea of self-attention and why positions must be added, and use DistilBERT's contextual vectors to tell the river bank from the high-street bank. Finally you'll map embedding spaces with PCA and t-SNE, test analogies and see where they mislead, and probe the social biases embeddings absorb. Every module has a lab with exact expected output, and the capstone trains word2vec and fastText on financial news and explores what they learned. It builds on NLP Foundations with Python and Corpora and prepares you for Transformers and Large Language Models.

modules.title: Vector space and basic vectorisation
modules.summary: Turn text into vectors a model can use: one-hot word vectors and why they fail, bags of words and n-grams, sparse storage, TF-IDF exactly as scikit-learn computes it, and feature hashing.

lessons.title: One-hot vectors and their limits
objectives: Build one-hot vectors from a vocabulary
Explain why one-hot vectors can't express similarity
key_points: A one-hot vector represents word number i of a vocabulary of size V as V zeros with a single 1 at position i, so its length grows with the vocabulary.

Every pair of different one-hot vectors is orthogonal, with a dot product and cosine of 0, so 'bread' is exactly as far from 'loaf' as from 'bike', and nothing learned about one word carries over to another.
A word outside the vocabulary has no one-hot vector at all; systems either drop it or map it to a shared unknown token.
Multiplying a one-hot vector by a V × d matrix just selects one row of the matrix, which is why an embedding layer is a lookup table: dense representations replace the one-hot vector with that row.

lessons.title: Bags of words and n-gram features
objectives: Represent documents as bags of words with CountVectorizer
Add n-grams and control the size of the vocabulary
key_points: A bag of words represents a document by how often each vocabulary word occurs in it and ignores order, so 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' get the same vector.
CountVectorizer learns the vocabulary in fit() and counts words in transform(); its vocabulary_ attribute maps each word to its column, and words not seen in fitting are ignored.

ngram_range=(1, 2) adds bigrams such as 'olive oil', which keep a little order and capture phrases and negations such as 'not good', but the feature count grows fast: in the lab's 30 notes, from 208 unigrams to 507 with bigrams and 792 with trigrams.
min_df and max_df drop words found in too few or too many documents, max_features keeps only the most frequent, and binary=True records whether a word occurs rather than how often.
Bags of words work well for topic and sentiment classification with linear models, but they can't relate synonyms or represent words they've never seen.

lessons.title: Sparsity and sparse matrices
objectives: Measure how sparse a document-term matrix is
Store and use sparse matrices without making them dense
key_points: Each document uses a tiny share of the vocabulary, so a document-term matrix is mostly zeros: the lab's 30 notes fill 329 of 6,240 cells, 5.3%, and real corpora are far sparser.

SciPy's CSR (compressed sparse row) format stores only the non-zero values and their column indices, plus one pointer per row, so memory grows with the non-zeros, not with rows × columns: 4,072 bytes instead of 49,920 for the lab's matrix.

Calling .toarray() on a large sparse matrix can exhaust memory, and so can operations that fill in the zeros, such as subtracting each column's mean, which is why StandardScaler needs with_mean=False for sparse input.
Linear models, Naive Bayes, nearest neighbours with cosine distance and TruncatedSVD in scikit-learn all accept sparse input directly.
Sparsity is a modelling problem too: in a small corpus most word pairs never occur together, so similarities estimated from sparse counts are noisy, which dense embeddings help with.

lessons.title: TF-IDF as a document representation
objectives: Reproduce scikit-learn's TF-IDF values by hand
Choose TF-IDF settings for a task, and hash features when the vocabulary is unbounded
key_points: scikit-learn's TfidfVectorizer multiplies each raw count by idf = ln((1 + n) / (1 + df)) + 1 by default (smooth_idf=True), where n is the number of documents, then scales every row to length 1 (norm='l2').
This differs from the textbook log(N / df): the smoothing acts as if one extra document contained every word, and the + 1 keeps words that occur in every document from getting a weight of 0.
Because rows have length 1, the dot product of two TF-IDF rows is their cosine similarity; sublinear_tf=True replaces a count c with 1 + ln(c), damping words that repeat.
Fit the vectoriser on the training documents only and reuse it for new ones; fitting on test documents leaks their document frequencies into the model.

HashingVectorizer maps each word to a column with a hash function, so it stores no vocabulary and suits streams, but different words can collide and columns can't be traced back to words: 24 of the lab's 208 words share a column when hashed into 1,024.

"""Represent 30 short notes four ways: one-hot word vectors, bag of words, TF-IDF and hashed features."""

import math
from collections import Counter

import numpy as np
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer, HashingVectorizer, TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity


def load(path="notes.tsv"):
    rows = [line.rstrip("\n").split("\t") for line in open(path, encoding="utf-8")]
    return [text for _, text in rows], [topic for topic, _ in rows]


def one_hot(word, vocabulary):
    # TODO 1: a vector of len(vocabulary) zeros with a 1 at the word's column, vocabulary[word]
    pass


def neighbour_agreement(matrix, topics):
    """Share of documents whose most similar other document has the same topic."""
    # TODO 4: cosine_similarity(matrix) for every pair, set the diagonal to -1 so a note isn't its own
    #         neighbour, take each row's argmax, and return the share whose neighbour has the same topic
    return 0.0


def main():
    texts, topics = load()
    bow = CountVectorizer()
    X = bow.fit_transform(texts)
    vocab = bow.vocabulary_
    print(f"{len(texts)} notes, vocabulary {len(vocab)} words")

    bread, loaf, bike = (one_hot(w, vocab) for w in ("bread", "loaf", "bike"))
    print(f"One-hot: {len(bread)} dimensions; cosine(bread, loaf) = {bread @ loaf:.1f}, cosine(bread, bike) = {bread @ bike:.1f}")

    for n in (1, 2, 3):
        size = len(CountVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, n)).fit(texts).vocabulary_)
        print(f"n-grams up to {n}: {size} features")

    density = X.nnz / (X.shape[0] * X.shape[1])
    # TODO 2: bytes for a dense float64 matrix of this shape (8 per cell), and for the CSR matrix
    #         (X.data.nbytes + X.indices.nbytes + X.indptr.nbytes)
    dense_bytes = sparse_bytes = 0
    print(f"Bag of words: shape {X.shape}, {X.nnz} non-zero ({density:.1%}); dense {dense_bytes} bytes, CSR {sparse_bytes} bytes")

    tfidf = TfidfVectorizer()
    T = tfidf.fit_transform(texts)
    doc, word = 3, "soup"
    analyse = tfidf.build_analyzer()  # the same lowercasing and tokenising the vectoriser uses
    # TODO 3: df = how many notes contain the word (use analyse(t)); idf = ln((1 + n) / (1 + df)) + 1;
    #         then count the words of note doc, weight each count by its idf (tfidf.idf_[tfidf.vocabulary_[w]]),
    #         and divide the word's weight by the length of the whole row (L2 normalisation)
    df, idf, by_hand = 0, 0.0, 0.0
    print(f"idf(soup): df={df}, by hand {idf:.4f}, scikit-learn {tfidf.idf_[tfidf.vocabulary_[word]]:.4f}")
    print(f"tf-idf of soup in note {doc}: by hand {by_hand:.4f}, scikit-learn {T[doc, tfidf.vocabulary_[word]]:.4f}")
    print(f"Row lengths after L2 normalisation: {np.round(np.sqrt(T.multiply(T).sum(axis=1)).A.ravel()[:3], 6)}")

    print(f"Nearest-neighbour topic agreement: counts {neighbour_agreement(X, topics):.3f}, "
          f"tf-idf {neighbour_agreement(T, topics):.3f}")
    sims = cosine_similarity(T[0], T).ravel()
    order = [i for i in np.argsort(-sims, kind="stable") if i != 0][:3]
    print("Closest to note 0:", [(int(i), topics[i], round(float(sims[i]), 3)) for i in order])

    hasher = HashingVectorizer(n_features=2 ** 10, alternate_sign=False, norm=None)
    # TODO 5: hash each vocabulary word on its own (hasher.transform([w]).indices[0] is its column),
    #         count how many words land in each bucket, and add up the words in buckets holding more than one
    buckets, shared = Counter(), 0
    print(f"Hashing {len(vocab)} words into 1024 buckets: {len(buckets)} buckets used, {shared} words share a bucket")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

modules.title: Word embeddings
modules.summary: Learn dense word vectors by prediction: word2vec's skip-gram and CBOW models, the negative sampling that makes them fast, and GloVe's global co-occurrence objective, trained from scratch and with gensim.

lessons.title: From counts to learned embeddings
objectives: Explain what a dense word embedding is
Contrast count-based and prediction-based embeddings
key_points: A word embedding is a dense vector of typically 50 to 300 real numbers per word, learned so that words used in similar contexts get similar vectors: the distributional hypothesis put to work.

Count-based methods build a co-occurrence matrix and reduce it, as PPMI with SVD does; prediction-based methods such as word2vec learn vectors by training a model to predict words from their neighbours.
Training is self-supervised: the signal comes from raw text, so embeddings can be trained on any large corpus without labels.
These are static embeddings: each word type gets one vector whatever its context, so the senses of 'bank' are blended into a single point.

Corpus size matters: trained on the 1 million words of the Brown corpus, word2vec gives 'violin' meaningless neighbours, while GloVe vectors trained on 6 billion tokens give 'cello', 'piano' and 'harpsichord'.

lessons.title: word2vec: skip-gram and CBOW
objectives: Describe the skip-gram and CBOW training tasks
Choose window size, dimensions and other word2vec settings
key_points: Skip-gram predicts each context word from the centre word, so every (centre, context) pair within the window is a training example; CBOW, the continuous bag of words, predicts the centre word from the average of its context vectors.
Each word has two vectors, one as a centre word and one as a context word, and usually only the centre (input) vectors are kept as the embeddings.

CBOW trains faster, while skip-gram usually represents rarer words better: on the Brown corpus, gensim's skip-gram gives 'tuesday' the other weekdays as neighbours, where CBOW's neighbours are mostly unrelated.
The window size changes what similarity means: small windows (2 to 5) favour words that can replace each other, larger ones words from the same topic.

Frequent words are subsampled, each occurrence dropped with a probability that grows with the word's frequency, which speeds training and helps rarer words; words below min_count are dropped entirely.

lessons.title: Negative sampling
objectives: Explain why a full softmax over the vocabulary is expensive
Write the skip-gram negative sampling objective
key_points: A full softmax needs a score for every vocabulary word at every training step, which is costly with hundreds of thousands of words; negative sampling replaces it with a few binary classifications.

For each true (word, context) pair, skip-gram with negative sampling (SGNS) maximises log σ(c · w) + Σ log σ(-n_i · w) over k negative words n_i drawn at random, pulling true contexts closer and pushing random words away.

Negatives are drawn from the unigram distribution raised to the power 0.75, which picks rare words more often than their frequency alone would; the word2vec paper suggests k of 5 to 20 for small datasets and 2 to 5 for large ones.
If the context vectors start at zero, every score is σ(0) = 0.5, so the loss for one positive and five negatives starts at 6 ln 2 ≈ 4.1589, a handy check that an implementation is wired correctly.
SGNS was later shown to implicitly factorise a word-context PMI matrix shifted by log k (Levy and Goldberg, 2014), linking it to the count-based methods.

lessons.title: GloVe: global co-occurrence statistics
objectives: Describe GloVe's training objective
Use pre-trained embeddings, and judge when to train your own
key_points: GloVe (Global Vectors; Pennington, Socher and Manning, 2014) fits word vectors so that the dot product of two words' vectors, plus two biases, approximates the logarithm of how often they co-occur across the whole corpus.

It minimises a weighted least-squares loss, Σ f(X_ij)(w_i · w̃_j + b_i + b̃_j - log X_ij)², where f(x) = (x / x_max)^0.75 below x_max = 100 and 1 above it, so very frequent pairs don't dominate and pairs that never co-occur are ignored.

The idea behind it is that ratios of co-occurrence probabilities carry meaning: 'solid' occurs far more often with 'ice' than with 'steam', while 'water' occurs with both, so the ratio separates the two.
Pre-trained GloVe vectors, such as the 400,000-word, 50-dimensional set trained on Wikipedia and Gigaword, load in one line with gensim.downloader.load('glove-wiki-gigaword-50').

Train your own embeddings when your domain's language differs from general text, as legal, medical or financial writing does, and you have enough of it; word2vec and GloVe give vectors of similar quality in practice.

"""Skip-gram with negative sampling, written in PyTorch and trained on the news section of the Brown corpus.

First, once:  python -c "import nltk; nltk.download('brown')"
"""

from collections import Counter

import torch
from nltk.corpus import brown
from torch import nn

WINDOW, DIM, NEGATIVES, EPOCHS, BATCH = 2, 50, 5, 3, 512


def build(min_count=5):
    sents = [[w.lower() for w in s if w.isalpha()] for s in brown.sents(categories="news")]
    freq = Counter(w for s in sents for w in s)
    vocab = sorted(w for w, c in freq.items() if c >= min_count)  # sorted, so every run numbers words the same way
    index = {w: i for i, w in enumerate(vocab)}
    pairs = []
    for s in sents:
        ids = [index[w] for w in s if w in index]
        for i, centre in enumerate(ids):
            for j in range(max(0, i - WINDOW), min(len(ids), i + WINDOW + 1)):
                if j != i:
                    pairs.append((centre, ids[j]))
    noise = torch.tensor([freq[w] for w in vocab], dtype=torch.float) ** 0.75  # unigram counts to the power 0.75
    return vocab, index, torch.tensor(pairs), noise / noise.sum()


class SkipGram(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_words, dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.words = nn.Embedding(n_words, dim)  # the vectors we keep
        self.contexts = nn.Embedding(n_words, dim)  # a second set, for words used as context
        nn.init.uniform_(self.words.weight, -0.5 / dim, 0.5 / dim)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.contexts.weight)

    def forward(self, centre, context, negatives):
        w = self.words(centre)  # (batch, dim)
        c = self.contexts(context)  # (batch, dim)
        n = self.contexts(negatives)  # (batch, k, dim)
        # TODO: the skip-gram negative sampling loss, averaged over the batch:
        #   -[ log σ(c · w) + Σ over the k negatives of log σ(-n · w) ]
        # nn.functional.logsigmoid gives log σ; (n @ w.unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1) gives the (batch, k) scores n · w
        raise NotImplementedError("write the loss")


def neighbours(model, vocab, index, word, k=5):
    vectors = nn.functional.normalize(model.words.weight.detach(), dim=1)
    sims = vectors @ vectors[index[word]]
    sims[index[word]] = -1
    return [vocab[i] for i in sims.topk(k).indices.tolist()]


def main():
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    vocab, index, pairs, noise = build()
    print(f"Vocabulary {len(vocab)} words, {len(pairs)} (centre, context) pairs")
    model = SkipGram(len(vocab), DIM)
    optimiser = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.01)
    with torch.no_grad():
        first = model(pairs[:BATCH, 0], pairs[:BATCH, 1], torch.multinomial(noise, BATCH * NEGATIVES, True).view(BATCH, -1))
    print(f"Loss before training: {first.item():.4f} (6 x ln 2 = 4.1589)")
    for epoch in range(1, EPOCHS + 1):
        order = torch.randperm(len(pairs))
        total, batches = 0.0, 0
        for start in range(0, len(pairs), BATCH):
            batch = pairs[order[start:start + BATCH]]
            negatives = torch.multinomial(noise, len(batch) * NEGATIVES, replacement=True).view(len(batch), -1)
            loss = model(batch[:, 0], batch[:, 1], negatives)
            optimiser.zero_grad()
            loss.backward()
            optimiser.step()
            total, batches = total + loss.item(), batches + 1
        print(f"Epoch {epoch}: mean loss {total / batches:.3f}")
    for word in ["monday", "president", "million"]:
        print(f"{word}: {neighbours(model, vocab, index, word)}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""word2vec with gensim on the Brown corpus, skip-gram and CBOW, compared with pre-trained GloVe vectors.

Run it with a fixed hash seed so gensim's results repeat:
  macOS/Linux:  PYTHONHASHSEED=0 python word2vec.py
  PowerShell:   $env:PYTHONHASHSEED=0; python word2vec.py
The first run downloads GloVe (66 MB) into ~/gensim-data.
"""

import time

import gensim.downloader as api
from gensim.models import Word2Vec
from nltk.corpus import brown

PROBES = ["tuesday", "week", "wife", "violin"]


def main():
    sents = [[w.lower() for w in s if w.isalpha()] for s in brown.sents()]
    print(f"{len(sents)} sentences, {sum(map(len, sents))} tokens")
    for name, sg in (("skip-gram", 1), ("CBOW", 0)):
        start = time.time()
        model = Word2Vec(sents, vector_size=100, window=5, min_count=5, sg=sg, negative=5, epochs=5,
                         workers=1, seed=42)
        print(f"{name}: vocabulary {len(model.wv)}, {model.wv.vector_size} dimensions, "
              f"trained in {time.time() - start:.0f} s")
        for word in PROBES:
            print(f"  {word}: {[w for w, _ in model.wv.most_similar(word, topn=5)]}")
        if sg:
            model.save("brown_skipgram.model")

    glove = api.load("glove-wiki-gigaword-50")
    print(f"GloVe (6 billion tokens of Wikipedia and Gigaword): {len(glove)} words, {glove.vector_size} dimensions")
    for word in PROBES:
        print(f"  {word}: {[w for w, _ in glove.most_similar(word, topn=5)]}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

If the first loss isn't 4.1589, check the signs: the positive term uses +score, the negative terms -score, and the loss is minus their mean.
If gensim's neighbours change between runs, the hash seed wasn't set before Python started, or workers isn't 1.

modules.title: Beyond words and universal representations
modules.summary: Handle words a model has never seen with subword embeddings, the fastText approach, then move from words to whole documents with averaged vectors, Doc2Vec and pre-trained sentence encoders.

lessons.title: The out-of-vocabulary problem
objectives: Explain why static word models fail on unseen words
Compare ways of handling out-of-vocabulary words
key_points: A word2vec or GloVe model has vectors only for the words in its training vocabulary, so a misspelling, a new name or a rare inflected form raises a KeyError or is mapped to one shared unknown vector.
Rare words inside the vocabulary suffer too: a word seen a handful of times gets a poorly trained vector, and min_count drops the rarest words altogether.
Morphologically rich languages such as Arabic, Turkish and Finnish have so many word forms that a large share of the words in any new text never appeared in training.
The remedies split words into smaller units, such as characters, character n-grams (fastText) or learned subword vocabularies (BPE, WordPiece), so a model can build a vector for any string.

lessons.title: Character n-grams and fastText
objectives: List the character n-grams fastText uses for a word
Explain how fastText builds vectors for unseen words, and where it misleads
key_points: fastText (Bojanowski and colleagues, 2017) represents a word by its character n-grams, of lengths 3 to 6 by default, with < and > marking the start and end, plus the whole word: the 3-grams of 'where' are '<wh', 'whe', 'her', 'ere' and 're>'.

A word's vector is the sum of its n-gram vectors and its own vector, trained with skip-gram or CBOW and negative sampling as in word2vec, so pieces shared by related words, such as prefixes and suffixes, are learned once.

To save memory, n-grams are hashed into a fixed number of buckets, 2 million by default, so distinct n-grams can share one; in gensim the bucket count times the dimensions sets most of the model's memory.

A word never seen in training still gets a vector from its n-grams: trained on Brown, fastText gives 'goverment' a cosine of 0.957 with 'government' and 'replayed' the neighbour 'played', where word2vec has no vector at all.
Shared n-grams also mislead: the same model ranks 'abandonment' above 'government' as the neighbour of 'goverment', because the '-ment' n-grams dominate the sum.

fastText helps most with morphology and typos, and not at all for words whose meaning isn't in their spelling, such as names; the separate fastText library also offers fast supervised text classification.

lessons.title: Document vectors: averages, SIF and Doc2Vec
objectives: Build document vectors by averaging word vectors
Explain how Doc2Vec learns paragraph vectors
key_points: The simplest document vector is the average of its word vectors: cheap and a strong baseline, but it ignores word order and lets frequent, uninformative words pull the average.
Weighted averages fix part of this: weighting by TF-IDF, or the SIF method (Arora, Liang and Ma, 2017), which weights each word by a / (a + p(w)) and removes the direction all sentences share.
Doc2Vec (Le and Mikolov, 2014) learns a vector for each document: in PV-DM it joins context word vectors to predict a missing word, and in PV-DBOW it alone predicts words sampled from the document.
A new document's vector must be inferred by gradient steps with the trained weights frozen (infer_vector in gensim), so it changes a little from one call to the next.

In the lab, the share of Brown documents whose nearest neighbour shares their category is 0.294 with TF-IDF, 0.348 with Doc2Vec and 0.376 with averaged fastText vectors: simple averages are hard to beat.

lessons.title: Universal sentence representations
objectives: Describe pre-trained sentence encoders and when to use them
key_points: A universal sentence representation is a fixed-size vector from a pre-trained encoder that works across many tasks without retraining, for similarity, clustering, retrieval or as features for a classifier.
Early examples learned from supervised tasks: InferSent from natural language inference data, and the Universal Sentence Encoder from several tasks at once.

Most sentence embeddings now come from transformer encoders fine-tuned for similarity, such as Sentence-BERT models trained on pairs of sentences; the next module explains the contextual vectors they're built from.

Choose by testing on your task: averaged static vectors are fast and need no GPU, while transformer encoders capture word order and context. Vector Databases and Semantic Search shows how to search millions of such vectors.

"""fastText's character n-grams, vectors for out-of-vocabulary words, and three kinds of document vector.

Run it with a fixed hash seed so gensim's results repeat:  PYTHONHASHSEED=0 python subwords.py
"""

import time

import numpy as np
from gensim.models import FastText
from gensim.models.doc2vec import Doc2Vec, TaggedDocument
from nltk.corpus import brown
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

OOV = ["goverment", "unfriendliness", "replayed"]


def char_ngrams(word, n_min=3, n_max=6):
    """The character n-grams fastText uses, with < and > marking the start and end of the word."""
    # TODO 1: add < and > around the word, then list every substring of length n_min to n_max, shorter ones first
    return []


def agreement(vectors, labels):
    """Share of documents whose most similar other document has the same Brown category."""
    # TODO 2: as in module 1's lab: cosine similarities, the diagonal set to -1, each row's argmax,
    #         and the share of documents whose nearest neighbour has the same label
    return 0.0


def main():
    print("3-grams of where:", char_ngrams("where", 3, 3))
    print(f"3- to 6-grams of where: {len(char_ngrams('where'))}, plus the word itself, <where>")

    sents = [[w.lower() for w in s if w.isalpha()] for s in brown.sents()]
    start = time.time()
    ft = FastText(sents, vector_size=100, window=5, min_count=5, sg=1, min_n=3, max_n=6, bucket=200_000, epochs=5,
                  workers=1, seed=42)
    print(f"fastText: vocabulary {len(ft.wv)}, trained in {time.time() - start:.0f} s")
    for word in OOV:
        print(f"  {word}: in vocabulary {word in ft.wv.key_to_index}, "
              f"neighbours {[w for w, _ in ft.wv.most_similar(word, topn=4)]}")
    print(f"  similarity(goverment, government) = {ft.wv.similarity('goverment', 'government'):.3f}")

    files = brown.fileids()
    labels = [brown.categories(fileids=f)[0] for f in files]
    docs = [[w.lower() for w in brown.words(fileids=f) if w.isalpha()] for f in files]
    tfidf = TfidfVectorizer(analyzer=lambda tokens: tokens, min_df=2).fit_transform(docs)
    averaged = np.array([np.mean([ft.wv[w] for w in d if w in ft.wv.key_to_index], axis=0) for d in docs])
    d2v = Doc2Vec([TaggedDocument(d, [i]) for i, d in enumerate(docs)], dm=0, vector_size=100, min_count=5,
                  epochs=20, workers=1, seed=42)
    paragraph = np.array([d2v.dv[i] for i in range(len(docs))])
    print(f"{len(docs)} Brown documents in {len(set(labels))} categories; nearest neighbour in the same category:")
    print(f"  TF-IDF {agreement(tfidf, labels):.3f}, averaged fastText vectors {agreement(averaged, labels):.3f}, "
          f"Doc2Vec PV-DBOW {agreement(paragraph, labels):.3f}")
    new = d2v.infer_vector(docs[0][:200], epochs=50)
    print(f"An inferred vector for a new text has {len(new)} numbers; most similar training document: "
          f"{labels[d2v.dv.most_similar([new], topn=1)[0][0]]}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

bucket=200_000 keeps the model to about 80 MB; gensim's default of 2,000,000 buckets needs about ten times as much memory.
infer_vector() starts from random values and runs gradient steps, so two calls give similar but not identical vectors.

modules.title: Transformer anatomy for contextual embeddings
modules.summary: See how transformers give every token a vector that depends on its sentence: the idea of self-attention, why positions must be added, how layers refine meaning, and how contextual vectors tell the senses of a word apart.

lessons.title: Static versus contextual embeddings
objectives: Explain how static and contextual embeddings differ
Get contextual vectors for words from a pre-trained encoder
key_points: A static embedding gives a word type one vector; a contextual embedding gives each occurrence its own vector, computed from the whole sentence, so 'bank' in 'river bank' and in 'bank account' gets different vectors.

Early contextual models such as ELMo (2018) used bidirectional LSTMs; transformer encoders such as BERT and its smaller distilled version, DistilBERT, now produce them, one vector per token from every layer.
Transformer tokenisers split rare words into subword pieces, so DistilBERT reads 'riverbank' as 'river' and '##bank'; for one vector per word, average its pieces or take the first.

With Hugging Face Transformers, AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained and AutoModel.from_pretrained load a checkpoint, and output_hidden_states=True returns every layer's vectors, from the embedding layer (index 0) to the last.
A model has a fixed maximum input (512 positions for BERT and DistilBERT), and its vectors aren't interchangeable with another model's, so compare vectors only from the same model and layer.

lessons.title: Self-attention, intuitively
objectives: Describe in words how self-attention mixes information between tokens
key_points: Self-attention lets every token look at every other token in the input and build its new vector as a weighted average of theirs, with the weights saying how relevant each one is.

The weights come from comparing a query computed from the current token with a key computed from each token, and the vectors averaged, the values, are a third projection of the tokens; the maths is covered in Transformers and Large Language Models.
In 'The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired', attention lets 'it' draw on 'animal', so the vector for 'it' carries information about what it refers to.
Several attention heads run in parallel, each free to track a different kind of relation, and stacked layers let later layers combine what earlier ones gathered.
Because every token attends to every other, the cost grows with the square of the input length, one reason models have a maximum length.

lessons.title: Positional encodings
objectives: Explain why transformers need positional information
Compare learned and fixed position encodings
key_points: Attention by itself ignores order: shuffle the words and each token gets the same weighted average as before, just in a different place, so 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' would look alike.
Transformers therefore add a position vector to each token's embedding before the first layer, so the same word at different positions starts from different vectors.

BERT and DistilBERT learn one position embedding for each of their 512 positions; the original transformer used fixed sine and cosine waves of different frequencies, and many recent models encode relative positions instead, for example with rotary embeddings.
Because the embedding layer already includes position, the layer-0 vectors of 'bank' in different sentences aren't identical: in the lab their cosines are about 0.96, whatever the sense.

lessons.title: Resolving polysemy with contextual vectors
objectives: Measure how well contextual vectors separate word senses
Disambiguate a word by comparing it with sense centroids
key_points: Polysemy, one word with several senses, is where contextual vectors shine: in DistilBERT's last layer, occurrences of 'bank' in the same sense have an average cosine of 0.850 against 0.627 across senses, while at the embedding layer both are about 0.96.

A simple word-sense disambiguator averages the vectors of a few labelled examples of each sense into centroids, and gives a new occurrence the sense of the nearest centroid; the lab's version gets both of its new sentences right.
Layers differ: lower layers stay close to the word and its position while higher layers carry more context, so test several layers rather than assuming the last is best.

Contextual vectors tend to crowd into a narrow cone, so even unrelated tokens have fairly high cosines; compare similarities with each other, or centre the vectors first, rather than reading absolute values.
A static vector leans towards a word's commonest sense: GloVe's single vector for 'bank' has 'banks', 'securities' and 'banking' as nearest neighbours, with no trace of rivers.

modules.title: Visualising and interpreting embeddings
modules.summary: Look inside embedding spaces with care: project them to two dimensions with PCA and t-SNE, measure similarity, test analogies and their pitfalls, and probe embeddings for social bias.

lessons.title: Principal component analysis
objectives: Project embeddings to two dimensions with PCA
Interpret explained variance and a PCA map
key_points: PCA finds the orthogonal directions along which the data varies most; projecting onto the first two gives a 2-D map that keeps as much of the variance as any linear projection can.

explained_variance_ratio_ says how much each component keeps: for 33 GloVe words from five groups (days, months, countries, colours and animals), two components keep 47.5% of the variance, so the map hides more than half.
PCA is linear, deterministic apart from the sign of each axis, and preserves large distances, so it shows global structure, such as which groups lie far apart, better than fine neighbourhoods.
scikit-learn's PCA centres the data itself; plot labelled points coloured by group, and check anything you conclude from the map against similarities in the full space.

lessons.title: t-SNE and the limits of maps
objectives: Make a t-SNE map of an embedding space
Avoid the common misreadings of t-SNE maps
key_points: t-SNE (van der Maaten and Hinton, 2008) places points in 2-D so that each point's near neighbours in the full space stay near it, matching neighbour probabilities with a heavy-tailed t distribution in the map.

Perplexity, roughly how many neighbours each point considers, is usually between 5 and 50 and must be smaller than the number of points; different values can give quite different pictures, so try several.

t-SNE is random: fix random_state for repeatable maps; init='pca', scikit-learn's default since version 1.2, gives steadier layouts, and in version 1.5 and later the iteration count is set with max_iter (it was n_iter).
The sizes of clusters and the distances between them in a t-SNE map mean little; only which points sit together is reliable. UMAP is a faster alternative with similar caveats.

lessons.title: Similarity, analogies and their pitfalls
objectives: Measure similarity with cosine in dense spaces
Solve and evaluate word analogies, and recognise their pitfalls
key_points: In a good space related words have high cosines: in GloVe, cosine(tuesday, wednesday) is 0.998 and cosine(cat, dog) 0.922, but tuesday and france still score 0.531, so unrelated words rarely come out near 0.
Analogies are solved with vector offsets: for a : b :: c : ?, find the word nearest to b - a + c. In GloVe, paris - france + italy gives rome.
The vector nearest to king - man + woman is king itself; the classic answer, queen, appears only because the method leaves out the input words, as gensim's most_similar does.

Analogy test sets such as Google's 19,544 questions measure accuracy by section, and gensim's evaluate_word_analogies scores a file in that format: on the lab's 146 questions GloVe gets 76.7%, with 53 of 56 capitals but only 14 of 30 past tenses.
Offsets work well for regular relations and poorly for others, and good analogy scores don't guarantee good results on a real task, so evaluate on the task as well.

lessons.title: Bias in embeddings and responsible use
objectives: Probe an embedding space for social bias
Explain the limits of debiasing, and use embeddings responsibly
key_points: Embeddings learn the associations in their training text, stereotypes included: Bolukbasi and colleagues (2016) found analogies such as man : computer programmer :: woman : homemaker in word2vec vectors trained on news.
A simple probe projects words onto a direction such as he - she: of ten occupations in GloVe, 'nurse' and 'receptionist' lie furthest towards 'she' and 'engineer' furthest towards 'he'.
The Word Embedding Association Test (Caliskan, Bryson and Narayanan, 2017) measures bias statistically, comparing how strongly two sets of target words associate with two sets of attribute words.

Removing a bias direction reduces what such probes detect, but much of the bias remains in the geometry, for example in which words cluster together (Gonen and Goldberg, 2019), so debiasing isn't a full fix.

Use embeddings responsibly: record the training data and its date, test for the biases that matter in your use, and respect communities' rights over text in their languages, as Māori data sovereignty principles set out.

Uses pre-trained GloVe vectors (66 MB, downloaded by gensim on the first run).
"""

}

        idx = [i for i, l in enumerate(labels) if l == group]
        ax.scatter(points[idx, 0], points[idx, 1], label=group)
        for i in idx:
            ax.annotate(words[i], points[i], fontsize=8)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.legend()
    fig.savefig(path, dpi=120, bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.close(fig)


def main():
    kv = api.load("glove-wiki-gigaword-50")
    words = [w for ws in GROUPS.values() for w in ws]
    labels = [g for g, ws in GROUPS.items() for _ in ws]
    X = np.array([kv[w] for w in words])

    pca = PCA(n_components=2)
    plot(pca.fit_transform(X), words, labels, "GloVe, PCA", "pca.png")
    print(f"{len(words)} words; PCA keeps {pca.explained_variance_ratio_.sum():.1%} of the variance in 2 dimensions")
    # TODO 1: a TSNE with n_components=2, perplexity=5, init="pca" and random_state=0, plotted to tsne.png;
    #         then print "Saved pca.png and tsne.png"

    for a, b in [("tuesday", "wednesday"), ("tuesday", "france"), ("cat", "dog"), ("cat", "purple")]:
        print(f"cosine({a}, {b}) = {kv.similarity(a, b):.3f}")

    # TODO 2: print the top 3 words for paris - france + italy with kv.most_similar(positive=..., negative=...);
    #         then for king - man + woman print the top 3 of kv.similar_by_vector(kv["king"] - kv["man"] + kv["woman"])
    #         ("inputs allowed") and of kv.most_similar ("inputs excluded")

    overall, sections = kv.evaluate_word_analogies("analogies.txt")
    for s in sections:
        if s["section"] != "Total accuracy":
            n_right, n_wrong = len(s["correct"]), len(s["incorrect"])
            print(f"  {s['section']}: {n_right}/{n_right + n_wrong}")
    print(f"Analogy accuracy: {overall:.3f}")

    # TODO 3: direction = kv["he"] - kv["she"], scaled to length 1; for each occupation, the cosine of its vector
    #         with the direction; print the occupations sorted from most negative (towards 'she'), with scores
    #         rounded to 3 places, after "Towards 'she' first:"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

study_plan.focus: Represent text as one-hot vectors, bags of words, TF-IDF and hashed features, and reproduce TF-IDF by hand.
Write skip-gram with negative sampling, train word2vec with gensim and compare it with GloVe.
Build vectors for unseen words with fastText, compare document vectors, and download the Reuters corpus for the capstone.
Extract contextual vectors from DistilBERT and use them to tell a word's senses apart.
Map and probe embedding spaces, build and submit the embedding space explorer, and review with the mock exam and the flashcards.

project.title: Embedding space explorer
project.brief: Explore how well static embeddings capture a specialised domain: financial news. Train a word2vec model and a fastText model, both skip-gram with negative sampling, on NLTK's Reuters corpus (nltk.download('reuters'), about 1.3 million words), with the same settings so the comparison is fair. Evaluate both on the starter file reuters_analogies.txt, 184 questions in four sections (country and currency, plurals, past tenses and comparatives), and add a section of at least 20 questions of your own from the domain. Show how fastText handles words it never saw, such as the misspellings 'governmnet', 'tradeing' and 'comapny', and where its character n-grams mislead. Then visualise the space with t-SNE and PCA maps of at least five domain clusters, such as currencies, commodities, countries, months and verbs of rising and falling, with notes on what they show and hide. In a reference run with 100 dimensions, a window of 5 and 5 epochs, fastText answered about 37% of the starter questions and word2vec about 27%, with the biggest gap on comparatives; explain the differences you find.
deliverables: train.py: preparing the Reuters sentences and training both models with fixed seeds, workers=1 and PYTHONHASHSEED set, saving both models
An evaluation table of accuracy per analogy section for both models, including your own section, with the questions each gets wrong examined
An out-of-vocabulary demonstration: at least six unseen words with fastText's nearest neighbours, failures included, and what word2vec does with the same words
At least two maps, t-SNE and PCA, of at least five labelled domain clusters, with the settings used
A two-page report: what each model captures, how and why they differ, what the maps show, and one risk or bias you'd check before using these vectors in a product

rubric.name: Training setup
rubric.description: Both models are trained on the same prepared corpus with matching, documented settings and fixed seeds, and the code runs end to end.

rubric.name: Analogy evaluation
rubric.description: Accuracy is reported per section for both models, the new section is sensible and within the vocabulary, and errors are analysed with examples.

rubric.name: Out-of-vocabulary handling
rubric.description: Unseen words are demonstrated with fastText's neighbours, failures as well as successes are explained in terms of character n-grams, and word2vec's lack of vectors is shown.

rubric.name: Visualisation
rubric.description: The maps are clear and labelled, the t-SNE perplexity is chosen and justified, and the notes don't over-read cluster sizes or distances.

rubric.name: Report
rubric.description: The report compares the models with evidence, explains the differences, and discusses a realistic risk or bias in the domain.

project.submit: Paste train.py and your evaluation code (or a repository link), the evaluation table, the out-of-vocabulary output, your maps (images or descriptions) and your report.
